CORDEBAUX DAM: Another view of the Cordeaux Dam which bestrides a huge valley and holds back millions of tons of water for Sydney to drink and bath and cook and wash its clothes in. The water in Cordeaux covers an area of 1931 acres to a depth of 170 ft.
THE GREAT WALL - BUT NOT IN CHINA. It holds back millions of tons of water in the Cordeaux Dam forming part of Sydney's drinking supply.

A MODERN TUTANKHAMEN. The ancient Egyptian could scarcely have slept more snugly in his tomb than does a resident of Sydney in the queer dwelling shown. It is situated in an unfrequented corner of the Municipal Golf Links, Moore Park. The flat, box-like erection on the right is the bedroom, reached by a burrow.

HAVE YOU SEEN OUR BRIDGE? will probably be Sydney's future formula of welcome for visitors. "The Sun's" photographer and artist have here collaborated on an aerial photograph of the harbor to give some idea of how the North Shore Bridge will appear. This bridge will span 1650 feet across the Harbor. The pylons measure 95ft x 50ft at their bases, tapering to 75ft x 34ft at their summit 810 feet above high water level.

SYTNEY HARBOR BRIDGE: The £5,000,000 contract secured by Messrs Dorman Long & Coy, Our picture shows construction work on the approach to the south side of the Harbor. This view was taken from the deck of a ferry steamer approaching Circular Quay. The contract for the bridge is to be completed by 1921. See other picture.

MAKING A LIFTING-SPAN This photograph shows how the lifting-span of the bridge over Middle Harbor at the Spit (Sydney) is being constructed. The bridge will shortly be open to traffic.
SYDNEY - SOME DAY, When the Sydney Harbor Bridge and the City underground railway are completed a few years hence, this is how the busiest part of the Harbor will appear.
SUNDABY'S UNDERGROUND BALMWAY. This view shows the construction of two tunnels which will take the underground trains from the main city circle out to the eastern suburbs.

An aerial view of Sydney Harbour taken from above Garden Island (the Naval Headquarters) The preliminary work on the bridge on the city side is seen in left middle distance while the approaches on the northern side are visible to right of picture. The long rectangular building on the northern side visible behind the orange represents the workshops established by Messrs Doman Long which are the biggest of their kind in the world. The total length of the arch and approach spans of the bridge will be 3,770 ft. while the central arch will have a open of 600ft with a clearance of 170 ft. above the bridge docking at high tide.

The first eating of the Federal Cabinet to be held at Canberra (New South Wales) Australia's Federal capital in the making, took place on January 30,1924 at Yarr-lumle Homestead, near the site of the future Capitol. GREAT SEWER WORK. The sewerage system of a big city is of remarkable magnitude. This is the opening of a tunnel, several miles long that is to convey but a small part of Sydney's sewerage from the North side of the Harbor only to the sea. The work is nearing completion.

SYDNEY'S UNDERGROUND RAILWAY. This shows a "tube" station in the City railway, and is in Hyde Park. First an open trench was excavated, and the platforms roughly constructed. Now it is being roofed over with a concrete arch. Next the earth will be filled in again, and Hyde Park will soon show little trace of the station beneath.

AMERICAN STEP TOBACCO THE FEDERAL CAPITAL. It is not often that a Minister performs the ceremony of stretching the first end with the aid of a clean church. But that is what Mr Steward (Fodor.) Minister for Works did at Gahanna on August 20, when he officially started work on the provision of Parliament House at Australia's Federal Capitol.

HUMAN SPIDERS. In this tangled steel web, riveters and their assistants move about with all the sureness of a spider in its eilken maze. This is a view, taken from the ground, of the dome of a new pavilion at the Royal Agricultural Shop Ground, Sydney.

SIDNEY'S CITY RAILWAY. The tonsil which will carry the trine under Hydrol Park is being used on the "oven out" plan. That is, a trench is dug, a arched tunnel is made at the bottom, and the earth is filled in again. This photo shows her the work he carried out.
The Federal Capital Territory 900 sq miles is included within the New border.

AUSTRALIA'S FIRST TUBE: A section of Sydney's underground railway was opened to traffic on December 20. It is modelled after the style of the London Tube and will go a long way to solving the traffic problem in this city of over 1,000,000 people.

TIN HARE ROOM OR ROOM. His is what those who go to the dogs in Sydney are asking since the new Premier Mr Bwin has declared he intends to make betting at night time illegal. However, this picture which shows a racecourse at Rosebery, near Sydney, being converted into a tin have track at a cost of about $45,000, seems to indicate that there is no need to take a gloomy view of things.
FROM THE AIR.
An aerial picture of Melbourne, showing the Flinders Street Railway terminus and the Yarra River.
GIANT BRIDGE: To walk across the Sydney Harbor Bridge when it is complete you will have to traverse a whole mile. O.P.S. One of the two footways provided for pedestrians. These are 10ft wide.

WORLDS BIGGEST ARCH BRIDGE: Work on the approach spans of Sydney's giant Harbor Bridge is now almost complete, and the construction of the enormous steel arch with a span of 1650ft (672ft longer than Hell Gate) which is to link the north side of the harbor with the main city - is about to commence. O.P.S. View looking across from north side to the city.
TAMING A CLOCK'S FACE. This queer photograph taken inside the dock tower of the G.P.C.Sydney, shows a man at work washing the face of the clock.

TUBE STATION IN THE MAKING: An interesting illustration of the making of an underground railway station. Under this concrete arch will be the Hyde Park station on Sydney's tube railway. When the roofing-over is finished and the connecting tunnels ready, the earth will be thrown in over the station, and Hyde Park will be restored to its natural beauty.

TUBE RAILWAY IN THE WAKING. This picture was taken from the site of the Hyde Park station in the Sydney underground railway system. The station will fill the whole of the cutting in the foreground. The tunnel in the background will carry trains to Circular Quay and through another tunnel branching off this one to the Eastern suburbs.

FORT DENISON was originally built in Sydney Harbor, near the mouth of Sydney Cève for defence purposes. In its early days it was used as a prison for the worst type of convicts. As a fortress it became obsolete 50 years ago. Its guns are rusted and the only inhabitants of its grim, underground vaults are hundreds of rats. But it still has several uses besides adding a picturesque touch to the Harbor. It serves to divide the incoming and outgoing traffic, and from it at 1 o'clock each day a gun is fired to keep Sydney's watches up to the mark. The picture was taken at the moment that the 1 o'clock gun was fired.

"Go to the mountains?" echoed the man in the clock. "Whadda you want to do that for? Plenty of ozone up here and you can run up and down the stairs if you feel like hill-climbing." He yelled the words to make his voice heard above the roaring wind.
"No," screamed the interviewer; "I said you'd be gone to the mountains if you fell from the girders—finished—smashed."

"Oh, there's not much chance of that, roared the man; "I'm used to it." The, as he regarded the hard footpath 200 feet below, he became practical. "But there aren't many mountains as flat as that plateau down there."

The man in the clock—or where the clock will be—a glazier. He and his mate are putting the glass on the four faces of the timepiece in the new tower of the Central Railway Station. You can see him from the street, sitting like a tiny spider in the round web of the girders. If you have the breath to climb the stairs which lead to his eryie you will find him a very intelligent, businesslike workman, who takes hair-raising risks to earn his three meals and a seat at the pictures now and again.
The Gale in the Tower

His intelligence was apparent. He didn't hail the interviewer as a representative of the capitalist and otherwise-to-be-despised adjectival Press. No; he grinned pleasantly, nodded and yelled "Good day."

Despite the gale, which screamed through the open tower and tore at the meshwork of girders, the glazier sat in the frame with most of his body over-handling streetway and juggled a lump of putty with one hand, while the other was engaged in keeping him from "crashing."
don't mind working up here. It's all right when you get used to it. I've been on high jobs before. Last one was at the Coast Hospital; they have a bit of a tower out there.
His lips moved again, but the gale put up an extra effort and the words went flying over the city towards where Baltimore lies in its corner of the harbor. "What?" yelled the interviewer.

The glazier climbed down and clawed across the tower against the wind. "We'll put the tarpaulin up," he shouted. "It's getting worse." A motheaten tarpaulin was rigged on the weather side of the clock face, and though the wind came through and around it, ricochetted off the corners and angled with a whistle off the roof, the pressure and noise was eased considerably.
"As I tried to say," said the man in the clock. "it looks small from below, doesn't it? But each of these faces is 15ft 9in in diameter—that's a bit smaller than the G.P.O. clock. I'm told. No we

The Peaceful Life

"There's advantages, too; no one to worry you--except the flaming wind, and that's been dead crook this week. Funny, y' know, to sit up here and watch the little people down there. Makes you feel bigger somehow and more important, and they're hurrying and scurrying about affairs that don't matter to us."

He indicated Pitt-street, which looked like a narrow, chasm between walls of shops. Directly beneath, a policeman was making laborious notes in his book and kept grabbing it as the wind ruffled the pages. He seemed all round cap and clutching hands. Behind him, two newsboys fought furiously, and a man, surrounded by an aura of dust, sped down the street in pursuit of his hat. And because all men chasing hats are funny, even when they don't look like square crabs with no legs, we two in the clock laughed.

Further over, in Central Square, midget people were rushing backwards and forwards, dodging toy trams and taxis. Two golden blobs showed where barrow merchants offered oranges for sale. And hanging over the whole panorama was dust in clouds which cluttered when the fugitive sunlight struck it.

"Oh, it's all right," he laughed, "there are plenty of hand and foot holds, and, anyhow, we have to do it sometimes. You see, these faces are double glazed. On the outside there's frosted glass to make it look white; then, inside, there's a backing of plain glass. This makes it watertight and we have to hang out there to get the frosted stuff in position. We cut all the glass here; it's sent up in bulk from the stores. It's just like fitting a jig-saw puzzle together. See, it's solidly fixed." He gave a set pane a hard smack to show it strength. "Nothing can shift. There's not a fraction of play in the girders as the bases are fixed into the stone."
Clean, Sweet Atmosphere
He dreams a little, does the man in the clock. The practical side of him is not always on top.

"It doesn't come up here," continued the glazier, referring to the dust. "Everything's clean and sweet here, and the breezes blow the cobwebs out of your brain. Yes, it's a bit cold early in the morning—more nappy than chilly: something like spray.
"I've been thinking," he broke out, "that they could make a good movie up here. Sensational--you know--something like The Glazier's Revenge or Who Stole the Wristlet Watch?
He waved his arms to show the spaciousness of the tower. It is about eighteen feet square and fifteen feet high.
"Work in a chase up the stairs; there's glazed slits in the wall of the tower all the way up that would give enough light."

"Perhaps you would," admitted the glazier. "They are a bit of a strain. But, anyhow, you could get a good struggle here with the town showing through the open girders and then a fight on the girders. Like this." He jumped to the frame, struggled through and climbed around the clock on the outside; a sheer fall of 200 feet beneath him if he missed a hold. His outstretched arms and legs made him look more like a spider than ever.

"This will be illuminated when finished and the hands will be illuminated too. They're going to fix an electric plant up here to regulate the hands and supply the light. Of course, there'll be a master clock downstairs to keep it in time. Four shafts will go out from the motor, one to each of the faces, and they'll rest on girders placed across the stone circles."

At the end of each of the twelve black bars which represent the figures is a small, red-glazed circle. This will show red during the night and help make the face plainer. There was some trouble about these red discs, the glazier said. One of the faces looks over the railway yard and the authorities thought drivers might mistake them for signals. But as they are hundreds of feet higher than the signals, there does not seem to be much danger.

The tower goes beyond the clock. "Come up and see it," invited the glazier. Up, there the gale was as busy as anywhere else, but a box-like structure which

"You should see the station from here in the busy times," the glazier said. "Early in the morning and late in the afternoon. It makes one wonder why there aren't more railway accidents. Trains come from nowhere—they just appear through the tunnel and wriggle along like brown snakes. Then they shoot off somewhere as if they were chasing something, and disappear under the platform roofs—just like snakes going into their holes. Hundreds of 'em coming and going, and they seem as if they will hit each other every few minutes."
He laughed as the absurdity struck him. "But you could, all the same," he went on, "Good light and plenty of room."
The Flagpole

More stairs led higher. At the top of them was a stone dome which boomed like a drum. The constant pounding of the wind accounted for this, and every word spoken ran around and around as though trying to get out. The strain on the ear drums was terrific.

Through the dome ran girders which support the flagpole. The pole is not attached to the stonework, but is given room to move when the wind hits it. Though it looks like a pencil from the street, the pole is 35ft in length. It is bound with sheet copper and a beaten copper scroll surrounds its base. Some workman who wishes to perpetuate his work has scratched his name on the scroll.
Back to the clock again, as the glazier had to continue his work. He juggled sheets of glass, which wriggled and flapped in the wind, and fixed them in position while he talked.

"Notice how close everything seems," he observed. "Look, there's North Sydney, and over there's the Heads, Bellevue Hill, Waverley, Randwick, Botany Bay, the University, and Balmain. You'd think you could step on Padding Town Hall, it seems so near. Bit different when you try to walk it.
Big Job Yet

"We'll be another week or so on the job yet; then the clock's got to be put into position. I dunno where that is. Don't think it's arrived in Sydney yet. When we finish glazing, there's another little treat in store. The girder frames have to be painted silver on the outside. That means swinging a painter's cradle from the top tower. Have to pick a calm day for the job, because if the cradle rocked or swung it might smash the glass; otherwise it's not risky."

Possibly it's not; but there can be more than one opinion about that. Below in the street the dust drove around and swallowed everything. Up in the clear air the spider on the clock faces hung through the girder web and waved a miniature arm in farewell.

MELBOURNE, Saturday.—No further information has been received with regard to Captain Stutt, one of the aviators who went out to search for the Amelia J. Measures are being taken to endeavor to locate the airman, and the police are conducting a search along the north-east coastal area, with H.M.A.S. Platypus assisting.

Major Anderson, the other aviator, is keeping in touch by wireless from his machine with the Platypus. Flying men are of the opinion that Captain Stutt, who is a skilled and experienced aviator, has been compelled to land at some inaccessible spot along the coast, where there is no telegraphic or telephonic facilities.

The soloist of the evening, Miss Reno Maxwell, took the audience storm. It is seldom that a singer has won spontaneous a welcome. Both her numbers, Depuis le jour (from Louise) by Charpentier, and Verdi's Ah Fors-e-lui (from Traviata) earned insistent encores, and Miss Maxwell had to sing each over again with the orchestra. The part of the hero, Lieut. Clive Stanton, V.C., is in the hands of Mr. Frank Harvey, who invests it with all the traditional casualness that masks a keen brain and an amazingly brave heart. THE DUKE TO OPEN AUSTRALIAN FEDERAL CAPITAL.

The stage is setting for the opening of Canberra, the Australian federal Capital, which will be opened by the Duke of York on Monday. The ceremonies will be broadcasted to 2,000,000 people. The Duke and Duchess of York will arrive on Sunday where they will be the guests of Lord Stonehaven, the Governor-General of Australia. O.P.S. A view of Canberra, the Federal Capital of Australia. PAGODA'S WANDERINGS - This Burmese Pagoda which cost £80,000 was sent from Rangoon to the great Wembley Exhibition. It has now been bought by a firm of mineral water makers (Schweppes) and brought to Australia where it is being re-executed to be used as a softdrink "bar" at the Sydney Showground.

MOVING A RIVER

The Arkansas River is to be moved from the center of the city of Huebla, Colo. to the outskirts, the position it occupied years ago. The project will cost $(4,000,000). Seepage causes this ditch to fill in as soon as the earth is removed by the drag machines, eight of which are in use. (from Keystone View Co.) BG
